title: Lifted as if in play
hookLine: a bow no king could lift, picked up as if it were nothing, and the sound that follows
carry: lila: what crushes kings is God's play

cards: The chest is open. The bow lies there, enormous. Nobody in the hall speaks.
Vishvamitra looks at Rama and says one short line: Rama, my son, look at the bow. No speech. Rama steps forward and asks, politely: may I touch it?
May I try to lift it, and string it? The king and the sage both say yes. And then, in front of thousands of people, something happens that Valmiki tells in only a few verses.

teach.b: Rama takes hold of the bow in the middle and lifts it, the text says, as if in play: the bow thousands of men just dragged in on a cart, the one a line of kings couldn't budge. He bends it and strings it.
He draws the string back, all the way to his ear.

teach.h: DRAWN TO THE EAR, IT BREAKS.
teach.b: And with a crack like thunder, the bow breaks in two. The earth shakes. Everyone in the hall falls to the ground, stunned, except four: Vishvamitra, King Janaka, Rama and Lakshmana.
Notice first that Rama asked before he touched it. No grabbing, no pride; that was yesterday's kings. Then notice that phrase, as if in play.

Later devotees heard a whole teaching in it: lila, divine play. In Hindu thought, God doesn't act out of need or strain. The world itself is often called God's lila, done freely and with joy, the way a child plays.
What crushes kings is play for the Lord.
That's why the plays that act out Rama's life every autumn, around Dussehra, are called Ramlila: Rama's play. In towns and temples people stage this very scene, and crowds cheer when the bow snaps.
When the people come to, Janaka is full of joy. I've seen Rama's strength with my own eyes, he says. Sita will bring glory to our family by marrying him.
My promise is fulfilled. He sends fast messengers to Ayodhya to bring King Dasharatha. The bow is broken.

how: The breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila performances and Ramayana recitations; in many places audiences cheer as the bow snaps, and the scene is often painted and sung at weddings.

o: the bow Rama asks to touch, then breaks in two
a bow Rama carries home to Ayodhya as a prize
the bow Lakshmana strings to test it before Rama

games.q: in the hall — tap the pairs.
p: Rama, my son, look at the bow
asks if he may touch it
breaks with a crack like thunder
divine play, done freely and with joy

s: Rama grabs the bow without asking
he asks the king and the sage if he may touch it and try.
everyone in the hall falls except four
Vishvamitra, Janaka, Rama and Lakshmana stay standing.
lila is divine play; the plays act out Rama's deeds, like the bow.

games.q: sam watches the bow scene at a ramlila and says 'so rama's just really strong?' what's the deeper answer?
o: for devotees it's lila: what crushes kings is God's play.
yes, it's a strength contest and he wins it.
the bow was old and already cracked.
games.why: Valmiki says he lifted it as if in play; devotees hear lila, God acting freely, without strain.

practice: Picture something heavy you've carried a long time, a worry, a task, a grudge. If you pray, hand it to Rama, or to God as you know God, for whom the bow was play.
If you don't, breathe in and lift it in your mind; breathe out and set it down, without forcing anything, as if in play.

wordCard.voice: Janaka's bow. Rama asks to touch it, lifts it as if in play, strings it, and draws it until it breaks with a crack like thunder.

orig.note: Sanskrit līlā: play, sport. in Hindu thought, God's free and joyful play; the root of Ramlila.

carryVoice: Your line: lila, what crushes kings is God's play. He asked first, then lifted it lightly. Day five hundred nine, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 67 (the bow lifted, strung and broken; Janaka's joy)
Brahma Sutra 2.1.33 (lokavat tu lila-kaivalyam: creation as mere play)
